caption:
Buying together? Up to $60,000 each. In Canada, the Home Buyers' Plan (HBP) lets each first-time buyer take up to $60,000 out of their own RRSP to buy a home, without paying tax on it, as long as they pay it back a bit each year.

WHY: the limit is per person, not per home. So a couple who both qualify and both have the money in their RRSPs can use up to $120,000 between them for the same home. The CRA's own first-home guide walks through a couple doing exactly this.

HOW:
1. Sign a written agreement to buy (or build) the home first.
2. Each of you fills in form T1036 (Home Buyers' Plan request) and gives it to the bank or provider that holds your RRSP. One form for each withdrawal.
3. Buy or build the home before October 1 of the year after your first withdrawal, and plan to live in it.
4. Pay it back a bit each year, over 15 years: at least 1/15 of the total a year once repayments start (after the grace period, per CRA). The CRA shows your minimum each year on your HBP statement of account, with your notice of assessment. You can always pay back more.

THE CATCH: it's a loan to yourself, not free money. You can only take what's already in your RRSP. Money you put into an RRSP in the 89 days before you take it out may not be deductible. A missed or short yearly payment is added to your income that year and taxed. And it all comes out of your retirement savings until you pay it back.

WHO THIS IS FOR: residents of Canada who count as first-time buyers: in the year you withdraw or the 4 years before it, you didn't live in a home that you owned. A home your current spouse or common-law partner owned counts too: if you lived in their home in that time, you don't qualify (CRA). Right now, for a first withdrawal from 2022 to 2028, repayments start the fifth year after it (CRA).

Do this: sign the deal to buy, then each ask your RRSP bank for form T1036.

Send this to the person you're house-hunting with.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #firsthome #homebuyersplan #rrsp #canadianmoney

caption:
Saving $0? Canada still adds $500. In Canada, the Canada Learning Bond puts $500 into a child's RESP for families with lower incomes, and you don't have to put in any money of your own.

WHY: the bond pays $500 for the first year your child qualifies, then $100 for each more year your family's income qualifies (based on the primary caregiver's adjusted family income), up to age 15. That's up to $2,000 in total. The bond is retroactive: amounts build up for each year of eligibility (to the end of the year the child turns 15), so years you missed aren't lost. An RESP (Registered Education Savings Plan) is a savings plan for school after high school. Personal contributions aren't required to get the bond. Canada also adds $25 to help cover the cost of opening the plan.

HOW:
1. Get a Social Insurance Number (SIN) for your child. It's free (Service Canada, or with the birth registration).
2. Pick a bank or other RESP provider that offers the Canada Learning Bond.
3. Open an RESP and ask them to apply for the bond. Bring your SIN and your child's.
4. Keep filing your taxes every year, so the CRA can see that your family still qualifies.

THE CATCH: you only get it if someone opens an RESP and asks. Each year is checked against family income, so some years may qualify and others not. The bond goes into one RESP per child. Kids born in 2024 or later: Canada plans to start opening one automatically from April 2028, but you can open one now.

WHO QUALIFIES: kids born in 2004 or later with a valid SIN, living in Canada, in a lower-income family. For July 2026 to June 2027, the family's adjusted income must be $58,523 or less with 1 to 3 children (under $66,036 with 4, under $73,577 with 5). Missed it as a kid? A young adult can still ask for it themselves until the day before they turn 21.

Do this: open an RESP and ask for the Canada Learning Bond.

Send this to a new parent.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #RESP #canadalearningbond #newparents #canadianmoney

caption:
Only 2 left? Sleep on it 24 hours. The habit: wait a day before you buy anything you didn't plan to.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 6. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHY IT WORKS: countdown timers and 'only 2 left' messages are built to rush you. Canada's Competition Bureau warns about fake urgency like this, where 'the timer runs out or resets but the offer is still available.' A one-day pause takes the rush away, so you decide with a clear head instead of a ticking clock.

HOW:
1. Leave it in the cart (or take a screenshot of it). Don't pay yet.
2. Set a phone reminder for the same time tomorrow: 'Still want it?'
3. When it goes off, buy it only if you still want it and it fits this month's budget.

THE CATCH: this is for wants, not needs. Groceries, rent and medicine don't wait a day. And sometimes a real sale does end; if it's gone tomorrow and you'd still pay full price, you didn't lose much.

Do this: next time a page says 'only 2 left', set a 24-hour reminder instead.

Send this to the friend with 12 open shopping tabs.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 7 lands Monday, Nov 9 at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.
